text: Lesson 25 gave you delivery performance. Lesson 26 gave you developer experience. Lesson 27 gave you the platform's own operational health. None of that is worth collecting if it just sits in a dashboard. The entire point of instrumenting all three is to answer one practical question every planning cycle: given everything we're seeing, what should we actually build next — not whatever the loudest team in Slack is asking for this week.

A few worked examples. If lead-time data shows every pipeline stage is fast except a manual security sign-off sitting open for two days, you don't need a survey — automate that gate. If one team's change failure rate runs three times the org average, the fix is targeted: better test coverage or a canary rollout for that specific pipeline, not a platform-wide initiative the data never actually called for.

No single number should greenlight a roadmap item by itself. A metric tells you where to look; it takes a conversation — interviews with a handful of engineers, recurring themes in support tickets, usage analytics showing which golden-path templates get abandoned half-finished — to tell you why it's happening, and whether the obvious automation is even the right fix for it.

Watch for Goodhart's law: once a measure becomes an explicit target, people optimize the measure instead of the goal it stood in for. If 'improve deployment frequency' becomes the stated mission, teams might split trivial changes into extra deploys just to move the number. The fix isn't to stop measuring — it's keeping DORA, SPACE, and platform telemetry in view together, so gaming one shows up as a gap against the others.

That's the whole arc of this chapter: measure delivery, measure experience, measure the platform's own services, and let all three together — confirmed against what people actually tell you — decide the backlog instead of a guess.

Chapter 8 puts everything from this entire course into one capstone build: a golden path template and service catalog entry, GitOps-driven progressive delivery for a real application, and the metrics from this chapter to know, with evidence instead of a guess, whether any of it actually worked.
